conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Und hier: ich? weich? Buch? hart?
conversation.translation: And here: ich? soft? Buch? hard?

lessons.description: German consonants follow a handful of steady rules. After this lesson you can attack any written German word and get its consonants right on the first try.
goals: Pronounce w, z, sch, and ß the German way.
Tell the two ch sounds apart: soft after i and e, throaty after a, o, u.
Start st- and sp- words with a built-in s: 'shtadt', 'schpielen'.
lessons.intro: German looks scary but its spelling is remarkably steady. The consonants carry a few steady rules: w is a v, z is a ts, sch is the English sh, and a word-initial st sounds like sht. The lines below are sound samples, not sentences: read them out loud and do not analyze them. With these rules you can sound out any German word - even one you have never heard.

phrases.translation: Sound sample: the German w is almost always a v-sound.
Sound sample: z and tz are both ts: 'tsahl', 'Plats'.
Sound sample: sch = sh; sp- at the start says 'shp'.
Sound sample: st- at the start says 'sht': 'shtadt'.
Sound sample: ch after i or e is a soft hissing sound.
Sound sample: ch after a, o, u is the throat 'loch' sound.
Sound sample: ss and ß are both a sharp s.

lessons.practicePrompt: Practice German consonant pronunciation with me. Use ONLY the sound samples from this lesson (word lists like 'Wasser, wann, warum'), never invented sentences. Ask me to read each sample out loud, then give feedback in English on specific consonant sounds: w, z, tz, sch, sp, st, both ch sounds, and ß. Keep everything very simple at A1 level.
lessons.title: Consonants: Read Them Right

vocabulary.usage: w says 'v': 'vaser'.
sch says 'sh' in native words.
ß is just a sharp s.
au sounds like 'ow' in 'now': 'haows'.
st- at the front says 'sht': 'shtuhl'.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.translation: Now: the vowels. Listening example: 'Staat' - long.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Ja: ei = 'ai'. Und ie = 'ii': Liebe, Tier.
conversation.translation: Yes: ei = 'eye'. And ie = 'ee': Liebe, Tier.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.translation: That is it. Very nice. More tomorrow.

lessons.description: The vowels carry the music of German. After this lesson you can handle ei vs ie, the eu 'oy', and the umlaut dots that pull every vowel forward.
goals: Say ei like 'eye', ie like 'ee', and eu like 'oy'.
Hear the long vs short difference: Staat vs Stadt.
Pronounce ä by moving a toward e; pronounce ö and ü with rounded lips.
lessons.intro: Now the vowels. Two rules do most of the work: a doubled vowel means long (der Staat), a consonant cluster after it means short (die Stadt). Then the digraphs: ei says 'eye', ie says 'ee', eu says 'oy' - and the umlaut dots do their own thing: ä moves a toward e; for ö and ü, say the vowel with rounded lips. The lines below are sound samples: read them out loud, do not analyze.

phrases.translation: Sound sample: in native words ei says 'eye'.
Sound sample: ie = long 'ee'; ü = 'ee' with rounded lips.
Sound sample: eu = 'oy'; ö = 'e' with rounded lips.
Sound sample: doubled aa = long; consonant cluster = short.
Sound sample: the umlauts ä, ö, ü - next to the plain a.
Sound sample: long u like 'Kuchen'; short u like 'put'.
Sound sample: ie is always long 'ee'.

lessons.practicePrompt: Practice German vowel sounds with me. Use ONLY the samples from this lesson (Staat/Stadt, Nein, Liebe, Tier, Kuchen, Käse, Tür, schön, grün). Ask me which vowel is long or short and how ei, ie, eu, ä, ö, ü sound. Give feedback in English. Keep everything at A1 level.
lessons.title: Vowels: Long, Short, and the Umlaut Dots

vocabulary.usage: The u runs long: 'Kuu-chen'. Compare eu = 'oy': Deutsch.
ä is an open e - like the e in 'bet'.
ei says 'eye' - 'iis'.
ü: say 'ee' with rounded lips.
o before nd often runs long.

lessons.description: Thousands of German words are one mouthful away from English. Bank the free ones now: they make every later conversation start above zero.
goals: Recognize international German words you already speak.
Say each cognate correctly using the consonant and vowel rules.
Start a habit of collecting free words in every new text you meet.
lessons.intro: German shares a huge international vocabulary with English - and English borrowed words like 'Kindergarten' from German. The words below are yours for free; you only need the sound rules from the last two lessons to say them well. Recognition today, real sentences soon: articles and verbs get their own lessons.

phrases.translation: Sound samples: three words you already speak.
Sound samples: same or nearly same spelling as English.
Sound samples: Kino is 'cinema' - a free word.
Sound sample: listen for the German stress - it can differ from English.
Sound samples: family words are international; Oma is grandma.
Sound samples: order these anywhere in Germany.
Sound sample: English borrowed this word from German.

lessons.practicePrompt: Quiz me on German words I already know from English (cognates). Say an English word like 'the computer', 'the bank', 'the cinema' and have me answer with the German word, then read a new cognate out loud using the sound rules. Correct only the pronunciation; do NOT test articles or sentences yet - those come in later lessons.
lessons.title: German You Already Know: Cognates

vocabulary.usage: Almost English: kom-PUU-ter.
Stress on the last syllable: ho-TEL.
Same word, German sound: 'tank'.
French word, French sound: 'res-to-RANG'.
Same spelling as English bank - the money kind too.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Hallo! Ich heiße Lena. Wie heißt du?
conversation.translation: Hello! My name is Lena. What is your name?

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Ich heiße Jonas. Und der Hund?
conversation.translation: My name is Jonas. And the dog?

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Der Tisch, der Hund, der Montag - alles 'der'!
conversation.translation: The table, the dog, Monday - all 'der'!

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Deutsch: Wort für Wort, Schritt für Schritt.
conversation.translation: German: word by word, step by step.

lessons.description: Many everyday nouns are masculine der - days and weekdays certainly are. With them you learn heißen, 'to be called': the verb of every German introduction.
goals: Say der with common masculine nouns.
Use the fixed name phrases: 'Wie heißt du?' - 'Ich heiße ...'.
Know that days of the week always take der.
lessons.intro: Every German noun wears an article, and the masculine one is der. Plenty of daily words are der: der Tisch, der Hund, der Mann - and all days of the week: der Montag. Your first verb is heißen, 'to be called'. 'Wie heißt du?' is one fixed phrase: learn it whole the way you learned 'Hallo'; the grammar of questions comes later.

phrases.translation: What is your name? (a fixed phrase - memorize it whole.)

phrases.text: Der Tisch, der Hund, der Mann.
phrases.translation: The table, the dog, the man. (all der)
Monday, Saturday. (days of the week are der)
The chair - broken. (fragment answers are fine in speech)

lessons.practicePrompt: Practice German masculine nouns and the name phrases with me. Say simple objects in English and ask me to answer with der + the German noun. Then rehearse the fixed exchange 'Wie heißt du?' - 'Ich heiße ...' without breaking it into parts. Correct only the article gender and the heißen forms.
lessons.title: Masculine Nouns: der and Your First Verb

vocabulary.usage: Masculine - always learn the article with the noun.
Many animal names are der - learn each noun with its article.
People match nature: der Mann.
Days of the week are der: der Montag, der Samstag.
Ich heiße, du heißt - your first verb. The 'he is called' form arrives with pronouns in Lesson 7.

lessons.description: The feminine family comes with a gift: two word endings make gender certain. Words in -ung and -heit are always die - a rule you will use every single day.
goals: Say die with common feminine nouns.
Trust -ung and -heit: words with those endings are always die.
Notice nature's own articles: die Sonne, der Mond.
lessons.intro: The feminine article is die, and German makes it unusually predictable: every word ending in -ung is die (die Zeitung), every word ending in -heit is die (die Freiheit). Collect the common die nouns on top of that: die Lampe, die Katze, die Sonne. Endings are German's quiet superpower - use them.

phrases.text: Die Lampe - an. Die Lampe - aus.
phrases.translation: The lamp - on. The lamp - off. (verbless: perfectly normal German)
The sun, the moon. (nature takes its own article)

lessons.practicePrompt: Practice German feminine nouns with me. Say English nouns - some plain (lamp, cat) and some whose German form ends in -ung or -heit (newspaper, freedom) - and ask me to answer with die + the German noun. Ask me why those endings are safe. Correct only the article and the ending rule.
lessons.title: Feminine Nouns: die

vocabulary.usage: Words ending in -ung are always die.
Words ending in -heit are always die.
A common household die-word.
Many animal names are die - learn the article with each noun.
Nature is not logical: die Sonne, but der Mond.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Und jetzt: 'das'. Das Buch, das Fenster.
conversation.translation: And now: 'das'. The book, the window.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Das Mädchen ... das Kind ... das Buch ...
conversation.translation: The girl ... the child ... the book ...

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Genau. Und die Welt? Der Mond, die Sonne.
conversation.translation: Exactly. And the world? The moon, the sun.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Der Mond? Der. Die Sonne? Die. Das Kind? Das.
conversation.translation: The moon? Der. The sun? Die. The child? Das.

lessons.description: The das family has its own guaranteed rule: every word in -chen is das. Finish the article trio here - from now on, every noun you meet can wear the right hat.
goals: Say das with common neuter nouns.
Apply the -chen rule: every diminutive is das.
Keep all three article families apart: der, die, das.
lessons.intro: Neuter is das: das Buch, das Fenster, das Kind. The famous rule is the little -chen: words in -chen are always das - even das Mädchen, the girl, because grammar is not logic. Many international words take das too: das Handy. With der, die, das behind you, learn each noun with its article from today on and every later lesson stays easier.

phrases.translation: The book - new. (verbless fragment: normal German)
Anna? 'The girl' is das - grammar over nature.
The cell phone - new. (many international words take das)

phrases.text: Der Mond, die Sonne, das Kind.
phrases.translation: The moon, the sun, the child. (each noun, its own article)

lessons.practicePrompt: Quiz me on German gender. Give me an English noun - sometimes one whose German form ends in -chen (girl), sometimes -ung or -heit (newspaper, freedom), sometimes plain - and ask me for the article and the rule behind it. Correct only the article choice and the ending rules.
lessons.title: Neuter Nouns: das, and Gender by Ending

vocabulary.usage: A core neuter noun: das Buch.
Words ending in -chen are always das - even this one.
Neuter: das Kind.
Neuter house word: das Fenster.
Many international words take das. German for 'cell phone'.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.translation: Ms. Keller - she is a teacher.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.translation: He is a student. Like us.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Er ist müde. Und ich bin müde. Und du?
conversation.translation: He is tired. And I am tired. And you?

lessons.description: ich, du, er, sie, es - the smallest words with the biggest job. The German twist: er/sie/es follow the noun's article, not nature.
goals: Use ich, du, er, sie, es, wir, ihr and sie (they).
Choose er/sie/es by the noun's article, not by its sex.
Use the frame 'Er/Sie/Es ist ...' and the fixed phrase 'Ich bin ...'.
lessons.intro: You know der, die, das - now they do double duty. When you point back at a noun, the pronoun copies its grammatical gender: der Tisch becomes er, die Katze becomes sie, das Kind becomes es. For people, nature usually agrees: er for a man, sie for a woman. The whole pronoun map is ich, du, er, sie, es, wir, ihr, sie. Everything today rides on one fixed frame, 'Er ist nett' - the full verb parade happens in the next lesson.

phrases.translation: I am Jonas. (one fixed phrase today - the full drill is Lesson 8.)
He is nice. (also 'it is nice' when the noun is der.)
She is a teacher. (also 'it is' for a die-noun.)
It is cold. (es without any noun behind it.)
The table? It is old. (er follows der.)
The cat? It is black. (sie follows die.)
The child? It is small. (es follows das.)
Mr. Weiß? He is a university student.
we, you all, they - the full set. (the matching verb forms come in Lesson 8)

lessons.practicePrompt: Play a meeting-new-people game with me: point at people and things using noun chunks with their article (der Hund, die Lampe, das Kind) and have me answer with the fixed frame 'Er/Sie/Es ist ...' or the memorized 'Ich bin ...'. Do not use question words yet - they are Lesson 14. Correct only the pronoun choice, especially er/sie/es for objects.
lessons.title: Who Is Who: Personal Pronouns

vocabulary.usage: Frau Keller = Ms. Keller; also 'the woman'.
Masculine; the female form is die Studentin.
Professions add -in for the female form.
Er ist nett. Sie ist nett. A word you will use daily.
Ich bin müde. Er ist müde. Guess how the class ends.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Er ist, sie ist, es ist. Und zusammen? Wir sind!
conversation.translation: He is, she is, it is. And together? We are!

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Und die Frage: Bist du bereit?
conversation.translation: And the question: Are you ready?

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Ich bin bereit. Und müde. Das bin ich immer!
conversation.translation: I am ready. And tired. That is me, always!

lessons.description: sein - to be - is the most-used verb in German, and completely irregular. Its six shapes are the first poem of the course: bin, bist, ist, sind, seid, sind.
goals: Conjugate sein for all six persons.
Flip sein into questions: Bist du ...? Seid ihr ...?
Use the pointer das: 'Das ist der Tisch' - 'Das bin ich'.
lessons.intro: German's engine is sein: ich bin, du bist, er ist, wir sind, ihr seid, sie sind. No trick makes it regular, so drill it like a poem - you just met its 'ist' form in the last lesson. Questions are only a word-order flip: Bist du bereit? And das is the universal pointer: Das ist der Tisch, das bin ich. After this lesson you can say who everyone and everything is.

phrases.translation: They are ready. (small sie, many people)
That is the table. (das, the pointer)
That is me. (point at a photo)

lessons.practicePrompt: Drill the verb sein with me: call out a subject (ich, du, der Hund, wir, ihr, sie alle) and ask me for the right sein form; then flip statements into questions (Bist du ...? Seid ihr ...?) and use the pointer das ('Das ist der Tisch', 'Das bin ich'). Correct only sein forms and the question flip.
lessons.title: Being Everything: the Verb sein

vocabulary.usage: Ich bin, du bist, er ist - irregular; drill it like a poem.
Bist du bereit? Seid ihr bereit?
Ich bin fertig! - I am done!
Alle müde? Ja, alle.
Wir sind hier. - We are here.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Dieser Stuhl ist neu. Nicht alt.
conversation.translation: This chair is new. Not old.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Dieses Wort: 'neu'. Der Stuhl ist neu.
conversation.translation: This word: 'new'. The chair is new.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Und das Buch? Dieses Buch ist super.
conversation.translation: And the book? This book is great.

lessons.description: Point like a German: dieser, diese, dieses copy the article of whatever you point at. Three words, and every object near you becomes conversation.
goals: Match dieser/diese/dieses to the noun's article.
Contrast plain der ('the') with dieser ('this one').
Point with short statements: 'Dieser Stuhl ist neu'.
lessons.intro: You already point with 'Das ist der Tisch'. The upgrade is dieser - 'this one' - and it just borrows the article you already know: dieser for der-words, diese for die-words, dieses for das-words. That is the whole lesson. Look around the room: every table, lamp and book is now a sentence waiting to happen.

phrases.text: Der Stuhl? Dieser Stuhl ist neu.
phrases.translation: The chair? This chair is new. (der = the, dieser = this one)
The word? This word is called 'old'.

lessons.practicePrompt: Play a pointing game with me: name an object with its article (der Stuhl, die Lampe, das Buch) and have me say a short statement 'Dieser/Diese/Dieses + noun + ist + adjective'. Keep every adjective after the verb - never an adjective directly before a noun. Correct only the dieser/diese/dieses choice.
lessons.title: This One, That One: dieser, diese, dieses

vocabulary.usage: der → dieser, die → diese, das → dieses.
Masculine: dieser Kurs.
Neuter: dieses Wort. A word worth knowing.
Ending -ung - you know the rule: die Übung.
Very common in spoken German - yes, like English.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Kaffee und Brot - wir haben alles!
conversation.translation: Coffee and bread - we have everything!

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.translation: Bruno always has everything. Dog luck!

lessons.description: German's second power verb, drilled early: ich habe, du hast, er hat. Tomorrow it meets its little friends.
goals: Conjugate haben for every person.
Answer 'Hast du ...?' and ask it yourself.
Use the German 'have' phrases: Hunger haben, Durst haben, Glück haben.
lessons.intro: haben (to have) is the verb of your daily life: ich habe, du hast, er hat, wir haben, ihr habt, sie haben. It is irregular in a famous way - the b disappears in du hast and er hat - so drill it today while it stands alone. Tomorrow: ein and kein, the two words that fit inside every haben sentence.

phrases.translation: He is hungry. (literally: he has hunger)
We are lucky. (literally: we have luck)
Bruno is hungry. (the dog from Lesson 4)

lessons.practicePrompt: Play my roommate: we are preparing a simple coffee break and check what we have. Ask me 'Hast du ...?' and let me answer with haben forms (ich habe, du hast, er hat...). Do not use a/no words or my/your words yet - those are the next two lessons. Correct only the haben forms.
lessons.title: Having It All: the Verb haben

vocabulary.usage: ich habe, du hast, er hat - the b disappears in du and er/sie/es.
German says 'Ich habe Hunger' for I am hungry.
'Habt ihr Durst?' - with drinks, a useful word.
'Zeit haben' - to have time. Use it daily.
'Glück haben' - to be lucky. Also: happiness.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.translation: No - not a book. A phone.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Ich habe kein Brot - nur ein Handy.
conversation.translation: I have no bread - only a phone.

lessons.description: The friendliest little words in German: one pattern - ein, eine, kein, keine - upgrades everything you already own.
goals: Use ein with der- and das-nouns, eine with die-nouns.
Negate any noun with kein or keine.
Answer about feminine and neuter objects with eine/ein or keine/kein.
lessons.intro: ein (a) marks one thing of its kind: ein Tisch, eine Lampe, ein Buch. kein (not a / no) is its negating twin: kein Problem, keine Zeit. Both borrow the article of the noun: der becomes ein, die becomes eine, das stays ein. Learn the pattern once - today you have or not-have half the room.
lessons.practicePrompt: Play a lost-and-found game with me: I say what I have or not-have using feminine and neuter nouns only. Ask me 'Hast du eine/ein ...?' and have me answer with eine/ein or keine/kein. Do not use masculine nouns or my/your words yet. Correct only the ein/kein pattern.
lessons.title: A and Not-A: ein and kein

vocabulary.usage: der → ein, die → eine, das → ein: ein Tisch, eine Lampe, ein Buch.
Negates a whole noun: kein Geld, keine Zeit.
'Hast du eine Frage?' - ask and answer.
Uncountable here - so: kein Brot.
Uncountable: 'Ich habe kein Geld.'

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Nein - das ist nicht meine Tasche.
conversation.translation: No - that is not my bag.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Meine auch! Und mein Buch ist hier.
conversation.translation: Mine too! And my book is here.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Kein Problem. Mein Kaffee ist noch warm.
conversation.translation: No problem. My coffee is still warm.

lessons.description: Possession is just the ein-family with an owner inside: mein Tisch, deine Lampe, mein Buch.
goals: Say my and your: mein, meine, dein, deine.
Ask 'Ist das dein/deine ...?' and answer it.
Keep the whole ein-family in one head: ein, kein, mein, dein.
lessons.intro: mein (my) and dein (your) join ein and kein in one family: der → mein Tisch, die → meine Lampe, das → mein Buch. The same endings you drilled yesterday, now carrying an owner - nothing new to learn, only new words to say. By the end of this lesson every object in the room can claim its owner.

phrases.text: Nein, das ist nicht meine Tasche.
phrases.translation: No, that is not my bag.

lessons.practicePrompt: Practice possession with me: name an object (with its der/die/das) and ask whose it is, so I answer with mein/dein + noun and the right -e ending. Ask 'Ist das dein/deine ...?' and let me confirm or deny. Correct only the mein/dein endings.
lessons.title: Mine and Yours: mein and dein

vocabulary.usage: mein Tisch, meine Lampe, mein Buch - watch the -e with die-nouns.
dein Hund, deine Katze - same pattern as mein.
A useful masculine noun: 'Ist dein Schlüssel hier?'
'Ist das deine Tasche?' - a phrase for every lost item.
Verbs and adjectives say nicht: 'Das ist nicht mein Buch.'

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Ja, ich arbeite hier. Und ich wohne hier.
conversation.translation: Yes, I work here. And I live here.

lessons.description: The German engine -e, -st, -t, -en: regular verbs click into place with almost no memory work.
goals: Conjugate regular verbs: -e, -st, -t, -en.
Use arbeiten, spielen, wohnen, lernen, machen correctly.
Recognize the formal Sie form: Arbeiten Sie hier?
lessons.intro: Regular verbs are mechanical: ich lerne, du lernst, er lernt, wir lernen, ihr lernt, sie lernen. Only -st (du) and -t (er/sie/es) demand real memory. Some verbs need a helper -e for the tongue: du arbeitest, not 'du arbeitst'. Today all sentences keep a clean start; questions with was and wo - and the famous second place - come next lesson.
lessons.practicePrompt: Chat with me about learning, working and living in German. Ask verb-first yes/no questions (Lernst du ...? Arbeitest du ...?) and drill regular verb endings -e, -st, -t, -en. Keep plain word order - no was/wo questions yet, they come next lesson. Correct only verb endings and the formal Sie.
lessons.title: Click: Regular Verb Endings

vocabulary.usage: The model verb: ich lerne, du lernst, er lernt.
Needs the helper -e: du arbeitest, er arbeitet.
Regular: du spielst, er spielt.
'Sie wohnt in Berlin.'
'Wir machen Musik.'

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Ich lerne Deutsch. Arbeitest du hier?
conversation.translation: I learn German. Do you work here?

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Ja, ich arbeite - und morgen lerne ich auch!
conversation.translation: Yes, I work - and tomorrow I learn too!

lessons.description: The law of German: the verb owns second place. Plus the w-words that open every real conversation.
goals: Ask open questions: was, wo, wer, wie.
Keep the verb in second position after time words.
Flip the subject behind the verb: Morgen lerne ich.
lessons.intro: Two powers today. One: the verb is always the second element - not the second word, the second element. Start with 'Morgen' and the subject must flip: Morgen arbeite ich. Two: the w-questions - was, wo, wer, wie - open questions that let you ask about everything you learned to say. Combine them and you are holding conversations, not phrases.

phrases.translation: Tomorrow I learn German. (verb second, subject flips)

phrases.text: Heute arbeiten wir, morgen lernen wir.
phrases.translation: Today we work, tomorrow we learn.

lessons.practicePrompt: Practice verb-second word order and w-questions with me: give me a time word (heute, morgen) and have me start a sentence with it, flipping the subject; then ask me open questions with was, wo, wer and wie about our course and city. Correct only the verb position and the question words.
lessons.title: Second Place and Open Questions

vocabulary.usage: 'Was machst du?' - the king of questions.
'Wo wohnst du?' - no case endings needed: wo stands alone.
'Wer ist das?' - point and ask.
'Wie heißt das?' - the vocabulary machine.
'Heute lernen wir.' Pair it with morgen: now and next.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Ich, der Kaffee, das Bett - ein Team.
conversation.translation: Me, the coffee, the bed - a team.

lessons.description: Some of the most common verbs change their vowel for du and er: du fährst, er schläft. Only the broken forms - learn them once.
goals: Use a→ä verbs correctly after du and er/sie/es.
Keep ich/wir forms plain: ich fahre, wir schlafen.
Talk about travel, sleep and carrying things.
lessons.intro: A handful of everyday verbs cannot keep their a in the du and er/sie/es forms: fahren becomes du fährst, schlafen becomes du schläfst, tragen becomes du trägst. The ich and wir forms stay clean - ich fahre, wir schlafen - so there are only two broken shapes per verb. They happen to be the shapes you will say all day.

phrases.translation: I am leaving today. (fahren: du fährst)
You sleep too much. (schlafen: du schläfst)
I am carrying my bag. (tragen: du trägst)

lessons.practicePrompt: Talk with me in German about weekends, travel and sleep. Make me use the a→ä verbs fahren, schlafen, tragen after du and er/sie/es, and keep ich/wir forms clean. Correct only the vowel-changing forms.
lessons.title: Breaking the Pattern: a Becomes ä

vocabulary.usage: a breaks: du fährst, er fährt - ich fahre stays clean.
a breaks: du schläfst, er schläft.
a breaks: du trägst, er trägt.
'Fährst du Samstag?' - a weekend question. Weekdays are der: der Samstag.
'Du schläfst zu viel.' - a polite sentence for friends.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Ein bisschen. Ich spreche Deutsch und ein bisschen Englisch.
conversation.translation: A little. I speak German and a little English.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.translation: And what do you like eating?

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Brot. Und ich lese gern. Immer.
conversation.translation: Bread. And I like reading. Always.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Lesen und essen? Das ist dein Ding.
conversation.translation: Reading and eating? That is your thing.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Sprechen? Das mache ich gern - danach.
conversation.translation: Speaking? I like doing that afterwards.

lessons.description: The second gang of vowel-changers: du sprichst, sie liest, du isst. e goes to i - or to ie.
goals: Use e→i and e→ie verbs after du and er/sie/es.
Conjugate essen, sprechen, lesen, nehmen in the breaking forms.
Talk about food and language.
lessons.intro: The same trick with e: sprechen becomes du sprichst, essen becomes du isst, lesen becomes du liest - the ie in liest says 'ee'. Take these four verbs with you - speak, read, eat, take - and daily life in German opens up. As before: only du and er/sie/es break; ich spreche is clean.

phrases.translation: He is reading a book. (lesen: du liest)
What do you like to read?
What are you eating? (essen: du isst)
Are you taking that? (nehmen: du nimmst)
We are eating bread and cake.

lessons.practicePrompt: Talk with me in German about food, reading and languages. Make me use the e-changing verbs sprechen, lesen, essen, nehmen in the du and er/sie/es forms. Help me place the magic word gern correctly. Correct only those verb forms.
lessons.title: More Pattern Breakers: e Becomes i

vocabulary.usage: e → i: du sprichst, er spricht.
e → ie: du liest, er liest - say it 'lee-st'.
e → i, and it doubles: du isst, er isst.
e → i: du nimmst - the n doubles too.
The magic word: 'Ich lese gern.' - I like reading.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.translation: Yes, it is getting cold fast.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Müde und kalt? Das Bett ist gut.
conversation.translation: Tired and cold? The bed is good.

lessons.description: Everything changes in German - and one verb + one tiny word describe it all: es wird kalt.
goals: Conjugate werden: du wirst, er wird.
Say what is changing with werden + adjective.
Use the impersonal es for weather and general states.
lessons.intro: werden (to become) is the verb of change: weather and mood - ich werde, du wirst, er wird, wir werden. Pair it with the empty, all-purpose es - it covers weather and general states with no noun behind it: Es regnet, es wird dunkel. Two tools for how everything around you turns different.
lessons.practicePrompt: Talk with me about weather, moods and changes in German. Ask me what is changing and how I am becoming, so I use werden (ich werde, du wirst, es wird) and the weather es: Es regnet, es wird kalt. Correct only werden forms and the impersonal es.
lessons.title: Becoming: werden and the Weather es

vocabulary.usage: The change verb: ich werde, du wirst, er wird.
The weather es: 'Es regnet.' - nobody does the raining.
'Es ist kalt' now; 'Es wird kalt' if the temperature moves.
The cozy half: 'Es wird warm.'
'Es wird dunkel.' - day to evening, in three words.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Die Tür ist offen. Du brauchst den Schlüssel nicht.
conversation.translation: The door is open. You do not need the key.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Stimmt! Ich sehe den Schlüssel. Da ist er!
conversation.translation: Right! I see the key. There it is!

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.translation: You often look for your key.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Sehr witzig. Ich brauche einen Kaffee.
conversation.translation: Very funny. I need a coffee.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Den Kaffee? Bitte - hier. Immer hier.
conversation.translation: The coffee? Please - here. Always here.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Kurs und Kaffee - das ist gut.
conversation.translation: Course and coffee - that is good.

lessons.description: When the action hits a thing, German shows it. Good news: only masculine changes anything.
goals: Use den and einen after the verb with masculine nouns.
Keep die/das nouns unchanged in the accusative.
Recognize accusative verb partners: sehen, brauchen, haben, suchen.
lessons.intro: The verb usually acts on something, and German marks that thing with the accusative. Only one gender advertises it: der becomes den, ein becomes einen, mein becomes meinen. The feminine and neuter articles you know stay exactly the same in the accusative - fight one gender, win two. The object pronouns mich and dich join in the next lesson.

phrases.translation: I have a brother. (ein → einen with masculine)
I see the man over there.
Are you looking for your key?
She is buying a book. (das - stays quiet)
You have a cat. (die - stays quiet)

lessons.practicePrompt: Play hide-and-seek with me in German: name things we lose, see, need or take, and make me say them in the accusative after verbs like sehen, brauchen, suchen, nehmen, haben - den, einen, meinen, deinen. Keep to masculine changes only; skip object pronouns like mich and dich, they come next lesson. Correct only the masculine accusative forms.
lessons.title: The Accusative: Only One Gender Cares

vocabulary.usage: der Mann → Ich sehe den Mann. The only loud change.
ein Hund → Ich habe einen Hund.
suchen + accusative: 'Ich suche den Schlüssel.'
Needs a thing: 'Ich brauche den Kaffee.'
Sehen + accusative: 'Ich sehe den Hund.'

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Wo bist du? Ich suche dich!
conversation.translation: Where are you? I am looking for you!

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Ja - ich sehe dich. Und ich sehe auch Bruno.
conversation.translation: Yes - I can see you. And I can see Bruno too.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.translation: Bruno? Are you looking for him too?

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Ich habe ihn! Er hat meinen Kaffee.
conversation.translation: I have him! He has my coffee.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Meinen Kaffee? Ich hole ihn sofort!
conversation.translation: My coffee? I am fetching him right now!

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Und der Kaffee? Ich brauche ihn!
conversation.translation: And the coffee? I need it!

lessons.description: After the verb, ich becomes mich and du becomes dich. Three tiny swaps - and hide-and-seek is fully grammatical.
goals: Use mich and dich after verbs.
Point back with ihn/sie/es following the noun's article.
Answer 'Siehst du mich?' with full pronoun sentences.
lessons.intro: The accusative touched only masculine articles - now it touches you. After the verb, ich becomes mich, du becomes dich, and pointing pronouns follow the article you know: der → ihn, die → sie, das → es. One rule decides everything: is someone or something receiving the action? Then it takes the object shape.

phrases.translation: The man? I see him. (der → ihn)
The cat? Everybody loves her. (die → sie)
The book? I have it. (das → es)
The child? I am calling it. (das → es)
I will pick you up later.

lessons.practicePrompt: Play a hide-and-seek scene with me: ask where people and things are, and make me answer with mich, dich, ihn, sie or es after the verb. Keep to singular nouns. Correct only the accusative pronouns.
lessons.title: Me and You, Him and Her: Object Pronouns

vocabulary.usage: The object form of ich: 'Siehst du mich?'
The object form of du: 'Ich sehe dich.'
The object form of er - and of every der-noun: der Hund → ihn.
The object form of sie - every die-noun: die Katze → sie.
The object form of das - das Kind → es.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Ein Geschenk für mich - sehr gut. Und Kaffee für dich?
conversation.translation: A gift for me - very good. And coffee for you?

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Und? Bist du gegen einen Spaziergang danach?
conversation.translation: And? Are you against a walk afterwards?

lessons.description: Three prepositions that always take the accusative - so the case you just learned now works on autopilot.
goals: Use für + person: für dich, für mich, für ihn.
Exclude things and people with ohne.
Say for or against something with für and gegen.
lessons.intro: für (for), ohne (without) and gegen (against) belong to the always-accusative club: whatever follows them takes the object shape you drilled last lesson - für dich, ohne mich, gegen den Plan. Three words, instant fluency.

phrases.text: Das Geschenk ist für meinen Bruder.
phrases.translation: The gift is for my brother.

lessons.practicePrompt: Order things and plans with me in German: who something is for (für + accusative), what it comes without (ohne + accusative), and whether we are for or against an idea (für/gegen + accusative). Correct only the preposition + accusative combinations.
lessons.title: For You, Without Sugar: für, ohne, gegen

vocabulary.usage: Always accusative: für mich, für dich, für ihn.
Also accusative: ohne dich, ohne Zucker.
Accusative too: gegen den Plan.
Neuter: das Geschenk - 'ein Geschenk für dich'.
'Ohne Bruno ist es langweilig.' - a dog's argument.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Die Lampen - neu. Die Tische - neu. Alles neu!
conversation.translation: The lamps - new. The tables - new. Everything new!

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Klassiker - das ist ein Kompliment. Danke.
conversation.translation: Classic - that is a compliment. Thanks.

lessons.description: German plurals have four main uniforms: -e, -er, -s and -n - plus umlaut surprises. Now the whole room can speak in plural.
goals: Form plurals with the four patterns: -e, -er, -s, -n.
Spot common umlaut plurals: Buch → Bücher, Apfel → Äpfel.
Use die with every plural - and keep -chen unchanged.
lessons.intro: Plurals in German are a family of patterns, not one rule: der Tisch → die Tische, das Buch → die Bücher (plural often adds an umlaut!), das Auto → die Autos (the international -s), die Lampe → die Lampen (the soft -n). And the -chen rule never dies: das Mädchen → die Mädchen - unchanged. die is the plural article for all of them.

phrases.translation: The book and the books. (u becomes ü + -er)
The table and the tables. (-e ending)
The lamp and the lamps. (the soft -n)
The car and the cars. (-s for international words)
The child and the children. (-er ending)

phrases.text: Das Mädchen und die Mädchen - alles gleich!
phrases.translation: The girl and the girls - the word stays the same!

lessons.practicePrompt: Quiz plurals with me: give me a singular noun with its article, and make me produce the plural with the right pattern (-e, -er, -s, -n, the umlaut, or the -chen trick). Correct only the plural form and the die article.
lessons.title: More Than One: the Plural Pack

vocabulary.usage: The famous umlaut pair: Buch → Bücher.
The most common plural ending: -e.
Feminine words love -n.
-s often appears with loanwords and many nouns ending in a vowel: das Auto → die Autos.
-chen words never change - but the article goes die in plural.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Dreißig - und neu hier. Wie ich!
conversation.translation: Thirty - and new here. Like me!

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Zwei Brüder. Meine Familie zählt vier.
conversation.translation: Two brothers. My family counts four.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Ich zähle drei: ich, Bruno - und mein Kaffee.
conversation.translation: I count three: me, Bruno - and my coffee.

lessons.description: German numbers run backwards - first the one, then the ten. Once that clicks, you can say your age, your family size and half the internet.
goals: Count: the teens, the decades, and the one-before-ten trick.
Say your age: Ich bin ... Jahre alt.
Ask Wie alt bist du? and Wie viele ... hast du?.
lessons.intro: Counting in German is arithmetic in reverse: achtundzwanzig means 'eight-and-twenty' - the one first, then the ten. The teens are the small rebels (elf, zwölf), the decades are tidy (zwanzig, dreißig, vierzig). Learn the pattern and counting becomes one rule wide. Today also finally answers 'Wie alt bist du?' - with years, brothers and sisters.

phrases.translation: I am 28 years old. (one first, then ten)

phrases.text: Ich habe zwei Brüder und eine Schwester.
phrases.translation: I have two brothers and a sister.
21 - first one, then twenty. The German way.

lessons.practicePrompt: Practice German numbers with me: I say numbers in English (up to 40, the teens and the decades) and you say them in German; ask me my age with 'Wie alt bist du?' and my family size with 'Wie viele ... hast du?'. Correct only the number words and the age sentence.
lessons.title: Counting: Numbers and Your Age

vocabulary.usage: 'Die Zahl' - and counting is zählen: 'Ich zähle bis zehn.'
'Wie alt bist du?' - age is old in German.
'Ich bin ... Jahre alt.' - use Jahre after a number when you say your age.
'Meine Nummer: null - sieben - vier.' Spoken digit by digit.
'Ich zähle: eins, zwei, drei ...' - counting in German.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Ich denke an gestern. Mein Bruder fragte: 'Morgen?' Und ich sagte: 'Ja.'
conversation.translation: I am thinking about yesterday. My brother asked: 'Tomorrow?' And I said: 'Yes.'

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Ja. Dann lernen wir zusammen - wie gestern.
conversation.translation: Yes. Then we study together - like yesterday.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Früher lernte ich allein. Immer allein.
conversation.translation: I used to study alone. Always alone.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Allein? Nie wieder! Morgen lernen wir zusammen.
conversation.translation: Alone? Never again! Tomorrow we study together.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Gut. Wir fragen, wir lernen - der beste Tag.
conversation.translation: Good. We ask, we learn - the best day.

lessons.description: German's written-story past: yesterday the verbs simply grow a -te. lernte, sagte, fragte, kauften - and suddenly you have a diary.
goals: Form the -te past: lernte, sagtest, kaufte, arbeitete.
Use the past time words: gestern, früher, damals.
Tell a whole small story about yesterday.
lessons.intro: German has two pasts, and this is the bookish one: regular verbs take -te plus personal endings: ich lernte, du lerntest, wir lernten, ihr lerntet - and no auxiliary verbs. Novels and stories live here. The spoken past with haben joins you later - today, write yesterday.

phrases.text: Gestern lernte ich den ganzen Tag.
phrases.translation: Yesterday I studied the whole day.
I used to study alone. (früher = in the past)

phrases.text: Wir fragten und lernten - den ganzen Tag.
phrases.translation: We asked and studied - the whole day.

lessons.practicePrompt: Remember yesterday with me: ask what I did, who said what, and what I did früher, so I answer in the -te past (lernte, sagte, fragte, kaufte, arbeitete). Only regular verbs - the famous irregular ones are the next lesson. Correct only the -te forms and the time words.
lessons.title: Telling Stories: the -te Past

vocabulary.usage: The story-starter word: 'Gestern lernte ich...'
'Früher lernte ich allein.' - before life got better.
'Damals fragte ich mehr.' - the nostalgia twin of früher.
ich sagte, du sagtest, wir sagten.
ich fragte, sie fragte: 'Wie heißt du?'
'Warum sagtest du das?' - the curiosity w-word.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.translation: And Tom? Did he come yesterday?

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Ja, er kam - und ging sofort wieder.
conversation.translation: Yes, he came - and left again right away.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Er sah meine Hausaufgaben - und ging.
conversation.translation: He saw my homework - and left.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Gut so. Wir sehen den Film allein!
conversation.translation: Good. We will watch the film alone!

lessons.description: The three most human verbs - go, come, see - refuse the -te pattern. Their past tense is short, strong and unforgettable.
goals: Use ging, kam, sah (and the du forms kamst, sahst).
Tell a two-sentence anecdote about yesterday.
Keep the other verbs on their -te pattern - no mixing.
lessons.intro: Yesterday the verbs grew endings; today three verbs change their soul: gehen → ging, kommen → kam, sehen → sah. No -te anywhere - these forms carry a new vowel and bare endings: ich ging, du kamst, er sah. They are the load-bearing verbs of every anecdote - go, come, see - so five minutes here unlocks a thousand stories.

phrases.text: Ich kam und ging - sehr schnell.
phrases.translation: I came and went - very fast.

lessons.practicePrompt: Tell me small yesterday-stories with gehen, kommen and sehen in the past (ging, kam, sah): ask me who came, who went and what someone saw. Save war and hatte for lesson 26 - they are not yours yet. Correct only the three strong past forms.
lessons.title: Story Verbs: ging, kam, sah

vocabulary.usage: Past: ich ging, du gingst, er ging. The anecdote king.
Past: ich kam, du kamst, er kam.
Past: ich sah, du sahst, er sah.
'Wir sahen einen Film.' - international word, German plot.
'Ich ging allein.' - and 'Nie wieder allein!'

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Für mich? Du gibst mir ein Geschenk?
conversation.translation: For me? You give me a gift?

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Ich gebe dir das Buch. Das Buch ist gut - wirklich!
conversation.translation: I am giving you the book. The book is good - really!

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Das ist mir wichtig - danke, Lena!
conversation.translation: That means a lot to me - thank you, Lena!

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Und Bruno? Ich gebe ihm auch etwas.
conversation.translation: And Bruno? I am giving him something too.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Ihm gibst du immer meinen Kaffee!
conversation.translation: You always give him my coffee!

lessons.description: The case of the receiver. After the giver, German says 'to whom' - and this time even the little n joins the party.
goals: Use mir, dir, ihm, ihr after verbs of giving and telling.
Form the dative articles: dem, der, den + plural -n.
Ask and answer the friendliest question: Wie geht es dir?.
lessons.intro: The accusative answers 'what?'; the dative answers 'to whom?'. Give, show, wish - the receiver wears the dative: ich gebe dir das Buch, er gibt mir den Schlüssel. The pronouns: ich → mir, du → dir, er → ihm, sie → ihr. The articles: der → dem, die → der, das → dem, and every plural grows an -n: den Kindern, den Männern. The accusative fought one gender; the dative gathers them all - learn the set once and German feels instantly more human.

phrases.translation: I give you the book. (dir = to you)
Do you give him the gift? (ihm = to him)
Do you give her the gift? (ihr = to her)

phrases.text: Der Kurs ist dem Mann wichtig.
phrases.translation: The course is important to the man. (der → dem)

phrases.text: Die Bücher sind den Kindern wichtig.
phrases.translation: The books are important to the children. (plural: den + -n)
How are you? (literally: how goes it to you)

lessons.practicePrompt: Practice the giver-and-receiver with me: give me things, then people (mir, dir, ihm, ihr), and say what is important to whom (Das ist mir/dir wichtig). Use geben and the dative articles dem/der/den+n. Object pronouns like mich/dich from lesson 19 are fair game too. Correct only the dative forms.
lessons.title: To Whom It May Concern: the Dative

vocabulary.usage: Two objects after geben: 'Ich gebe dir das Buch.' - thing in accusative, person in dative.
The dative of ich: 'Das ist mir wichtig.'
The dative of du: 'Wie geht es dir?'
The dative of er and sie: 'Ich gebe ihm/ihr das Buch.'
der Mann → dem Mann; das Kind → dem Kind. The dative article.
'Das ist mir wichtig.' - three words, deep feeling.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Kaffee ohne mich? Das war schade.
conversation.translation: Coffee without me? That was a shame.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Sehr schön. Kaffee heute - und Bruno war auch da.
conversation.translation: Great. Coffee today - and Bruno was there too.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.translation: And did my coffee get cold?

lessons.description: The past tense Germans actually speak every day: I was, I had, it became. Three small words, every yesterday covered.
goals: Use war: ich war, du warst, er war, wir waren.
Use hatte for what yesterday contained.
Use wurde to say what changed.
lessons.intro: Stories need their load-bearing walls, and these are them: sein becomes war (ich war, du warst, er war), haben becomes hatte, werden becomes wurde. The stems change once, then take past endings: ich war, du warst, wir waren; ich hatte, du hattest; ich wurde, du wurdest. They are also the verbs you use most: yesterday's state, yesterday's things, yesterday's changes.

phrases.translation: We were done - all of us!

lessons.practicePrompt: Talk about yesterday with me using the big three: ask whether I was sick, what I had, and what changed around me (war, hatte, wurde). Regular -te verbs from the last lessons are fair game too. Correct only the war/hatte/wurde forms.
lessons.title: Yesterday's Big Three: war, hatte, wurde

vocabulary.usage: The past of bin/ist: ich war, du warst, er war. Learn all three now.
The past of habe/hat: ich hatte, du hattest, er hatte.
The past of wird: es wurde kalt, er wurde müde.
'Warst du krank?' - the classic excuse. gesund is its twin.
'Bruno war da.' - the little pointer of place.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Ich kenne es nicht. Und ich weiß nichts.
conversation.translation: I do not know it. And I know nothing.

conversation.speaker: Jonas
conversation.text: Wir fragen Bruno. Er kennt alles.
conversation.translation: We ask Bruno. He knows everything.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Bruno weiß nichts - er schläft nur.
conversation.translation: Bruno knows nothing - he just sleeps.

conversation.speaker: Lena
conversation.text: Ich weiß: Dieser Kurs ist gut.
conversation.translation: I know: this course is good.

lessons.description: English knows everything with one verb. German asks: a fact or a face? wissen or kennen?
goals: Use wissen for facts: ich weiß, du weißt, er weiß.
Use kennen for people, places and things: kennst du ...?
Answer both with the full verb, not just ja or nein.
lessons.intro: German splits knowledge in two. wissen knows facts and answers: ich weiß, du weißt, er weiß (yes, the vowel breaks for du and er). kennen knows people, places and things by acquaintance: ich kenne, du kennst - perfectly regular, like the verbs of lesson 13. 'Weißt du, wer Bruno ist?' asks for a fact about Bruno; 'Kennst du Bruno?' asks whether he is your friend. One question, two worlds.
lessons.practicePrompt: Play quiz master with me: fire facts and faces at me - for facts use wissen ('Weißt du das?'), for people, places and things kennen ('Kennst du Bruno?'). I answer with ich weiß / ich kenne. Correct only the wissen and kennen forms.
lessons.title: Two Ways to Know: wissen and kennen

vocabulary.usage: ich weiß, du weißt, er weiß - the vowel breaks like in Lesson 16.
ich kenne, du kennst - regular and friendly.
kennen + places: 'Wir kennen die Stadt.'
'Er weiß alles.' - and nichts is its opposite.
'Ich weiß nichts.' - the honest answer.
'Ich kenne das Wort nicht.' - the survival phrase of this whole course.
